questions.explanation: Accuracy is correct predictions / total. Two of the three predictions match, so 2 / 3 ≈ 0.67.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Rows are the actual class, columns the predicted class: `[[TN, FP], [FN, TP]]`. Actual 0: one predicted 0 (TN) and one predicted 1 (FP). Actual 1: one predicted 0 (FN) and two predicted 1 (TP).

questions.question: A spam filter marks an important e-mail from your manager as spam. What kind of error is this?
options: A false positive (type I error, a false alarm)
A false negative (type II error, a missed case)
A true positive
A true negative
questions.explanation: "Spam" is the positive class. The model predicted positive while the e-mail was actually negative: a false positive, also called a type I error or false alarm.

questions.question: A disease test says a sick patient is healthy. What kind of error is this?
options: A false negative (type II error, a missed case)
A false positive (type I error, a false alarm)
A true negative
A true positive
questions.explanation: The patient is actually positive, but the model predicted negative: a false negative, also called a type II error. In medicine this is often the costliest mistake.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: TP = 2, FP = 1, FN = 2. Precision = TP / (TP + FP) = 2 / 3 ≈ 0.67: of everything flagged, how much was right. Recall = TP / (TP + FN) = 2 / 4 = 0.5: of all real positives, how many were found.

questions.question: scikit-learn has no `specificity_score`. What does this print?
code: tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred).ravel()
questions.explanation: Specificity = TN / (TN + FP) = 5 / 6 ≈ 0.83: recall for the negative class. `.ravel()` on a 2×2 confusion matrix gives the four counts in the order TN, FP, FN, TP.

questions.question: Precision is 2/3 and recall is 0.5. What does this print?
questions.explanation: F1 = 2 · precision · recall / (precision + recall) = 2 · 0.667 · 0.5 / 1.167 ≈ 0.57. It is the harmonic mean, which sits below the plain average (0.58) and punishes a weak score on either side.

questions.question: For which model is **precision** the most important metric?
options: A spam filter, where a real e-mail in the spam folder is costly
A cancer screening test, where a missed tumour is costly
A fraud detector, where missed fraud is costly
A model on perfectly balanced data, where all errors cost the same
questions.explanation: Precision answers "of everything I flagged, how much was right?", so it matters when false alarms are costly. Screening and fraud are about finding every real case, which is recall.

questions.question: When is **recall** (sensitivity) the metric to watch?
options: When missing a real positive is costly, as with fraud or disease
When false alarms are costly
When the classes are perfectly balanced
When you are predicting a continuous number
questions.explanation: Recall = TP / (TP + FN): of all real positives, how many did you find? It is the metric for problems where a missed case (false negative) hurts most.

questions.question: A fraud model scores 99 % accuracy on data with 1 % fraud. Why is that meaningless, and what should you report?
options: Predicting "no fraud" for everyone also scores 99 %; report precision, recall and F1 for the fraud class
99 % is excellent; accuracy is the best metric for fraud
The model must be overfitting; report the training accuracy too
Accuracy is only meaningless for regression; report R²
questions.explanation: On imbalanced data the majority class alone gives a high accuracy. Precision, recall and F1 for the rare class (and the confusion matrix) show whether the model actually catches fraud.

questions.question: You raise the classification threshold (drempel) from 0.5 to 0.8. What usually happens?
options: Precision goes up, recall goes down
Precision goes down, recall goes up
Both go up
Nothing; the threshold doesn't affect the metrics
questions.explanation: A higher threshold means the model only predicts 1 when it is very sure. Fewer false alarms raise precision, but more real positives are missed, so recall falls.

questions.question: `proba` holds the predicted probabilities of class 1. What does this print?
questions.explanation: With a threshold of 0.6, only 0.70 and 0.90 become class 1. With the default 0.5, 0.55 would also have been 1. This is how you apply a custom threshold to `predict_proba()` output.

questions.question: What does a **ROC curve** plot?
options: The true positive rate (recall) against the false positive rate, for all thresholds
Precision against recall, for the default threshold only
Training accuracy against test accuracy
The predicted value against the actual value
questions.explanation: The ROC curve shows the trade-off between catching positives (TPR) and raising false alarms (FPR) as you move the threshold from 1 down to 0.

questions.question: A classifier has ROC-AUC 0.5. What does that mean?
options: It is no better than random guessing
It is right half the time on the test set
It is perfect
Its threshold is set to 0.5
questions.explanation: AUC is the area under the ROC curve: 0.5 is random guessing and 1.0 is perfect. Because it covers all thresholds, it is a threshold-independent way to compare classifiers.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: AUC is the chance that a random positive gets a higher score than a random negative. Of the 4 positive-negative pairs, 3 are ordered correctly; only 0.35 (positive) < 0.4 (negative) is wrong. 3 / 4 = 0.75.
